sections.html:
Wisconsin dropped its estate tax for anyone who died on or after January 1, 2008. The old inheritance tax return covered only deaths before January 1, 1992. So a family taking over a house from a recent death owes no state tax for the deed passing to them.

An heir who plans to sell can still face other bills. There is the federal estate tax (only for very large estates), income tax on profit from the sale, and a county transfer fee charged when a deed is recorded. Each follows separate rules, taken up next. For a death before those cutoff years, the Department of Revenue can say which return applied.

A single house almost never triggers it. A federal return is due only when the gross estate, adding adjusted taxable gifts and the specific gift tax exemption, tops the filing threshold for the year of death. The figure is $15,000,000 for 2026, $13,990,000 for 2025 and $13,610,000 for 2024.

Gross estate means everything the person owned or held certain interests in, at fair market value on the date of death. Debts such as a mortgage, costs of administering the estate, and property going to a surviving spouse or a qualified charity are subtracted. Most relatively simple estates have no filing duty.

One more detail: a surviving spouse can choose to carry over the decedent's unused exemption, but only by electing on an estate tax return filed on time. If the estate you are settling comes close to the threshold, hire an estate attorney or tax preparer. A title company will not handle this.

Profit from the sale is taxable, though Wisconsin softens it. Capital asset gains and losses are reported on both the state and federal returns. For assets held longer than one year, the state generally lets you deduct 30% of the net capital gain. The Department of Revenue's Publication 103 is written for 2025 returns.

Gain equals the sale price minus basis. Basis normally means what the owner paid, but inherited property follows separate rules found in IRS Publication 551. Have the estate's tax preparer pin down the basis before you weigh offers, since it sets the tax result.

  • Individual heirs use Wisconsin Schedule WD. Estates and trusts use Schedule 2WD attached to Form 2, Wisconsin Fiduciary Income Tax for Estates and Trusts.
  • On a Wisconsin return, a net capital loss offsets up to $3,000 of other income ($1,500 for married filing separately), starting with tax year 2023. Bigger losses carry forward.
  • State and federal basis sometimes differ. Ask the preparer if an adjustment is needed.

The rate is 30 cents per $100 of value, and the seller owes it. Wis. Stat. 77.22(1) has the register of deeds take payment when the deed is handed in to be recorded, together with a transfer return signed by both parties to the deed.

Inheriting is not selling. When the house moves to heirs by will, descent or survivorship, Wis. Stat. 77.25(11) exempts it. When the estate sells to an outside buyer, no exemption applies and the price is what gets charged.

Transfer typeHow the fee applies
Estate or heirs sell to a buyerFee on the sale price
House goes to heirs by will, descent or survivorshipExempt
One heir pays siblings or the estate to keep the houseFee on the amount paid, exemption for the rest
Trustee deeds to a beneficiary, no paymentExempt
Gift between parent and child, or grandparent and grandchild, for nominal or no considerationExempt

Returns go in electronically unless a hardship waiver is granted. If a deed claims an exemption, it must name the 77.25 subsection right on its face.

sections.h2: Small estates and the affidavit route
sections.html:
Only small estates qualify. Wis. Stat. 867.03 allows collection by affidavit by certain people (an heir, a revocable trust's trustee, the will's named personal representative, the decedent's guardian) if the Wisconsin property subject to administration is worth no more than $50,000 gross. A house valued above that figure takes the estate out of the affidavit route on its own.

The named personal representative cannot take real estate this way unless also an heir, the trustee of the decedent's own revocable trust, or the guardian. A representative outside those categories waits 30 days after the affidavit is received. Bigger estates need a full probate case. Before a buyer can close, call the circuit court's probate office in the decedent's home county and ask what paperwork it wants.

sections.h2: How an estate sale usually unfolds
sections.html:
Order matters here, because each step feeds the next. Start by finding out whether probate is needed at all, since that decides who can sign. If the estate is small enough for an affidavit, the heir collects the house that way. If not, the court appoints someone with authority, and a buyer will want proof of it before closing.

Next comes the tax picture. The preparer sets the basis, estimates any gain, and tells you whether a federal return is even in question. With that number in hand you can compare a cash offer against a listing without guessing about what you would keep after taxes.

At closing, the seller's side of the statement carries the transfer fee, and the register of deeds takes the transfer return when the deed is recorded. Heirs who are buying out other heirs should raise that with the preparer before the deed is drafted, so the exemption wording is right. Bring the death certificate details, the deed, and any court paperwork that shows who speaks for the estate.

sections.h2: Before you accept a cash offer on an inherited house
sections.html:
Selling for cash is still selling, so the fee and gain rules above stay in play. Run through these before signing:

  • Get the house's basis and a rough gain figure from the estate's tax preparer, plus the schedule that reports it.
  • Ask the register of deeds in the county how the transfer return and exemption number should read on a deed moving title to heirs with no payment.
  • Put in writing who may sign for the estate. Ask the probate office what proof of that authority a buyer will expect.
  • Make sure the closing statement shows the transfer fee as a seller charge.
  • If one heir is buying out the others, tell the preparer. That payment carries the fee.

A cash sale avoids lender appraisals and financing delays. It does not avoid these tasks. Finish them first and closing day goes quickly.

faqs.q: Does Wisconsin have an inheritance tax?
faqs.a: No. The inheritance tax return covered only deaths before January 1, 1992, and Wisconsin has no estate tax for deaths on or after January 1, 2008. Someone inheriting a house from a recent death owes neither on the transfer.

faqs.q: How large must an estate be before a federal estate tax return is required?
faqs.a: For a 2026 death the threshold is $15,000,000. The gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts and the specific gift tax exemption is measured against it. Most relatively simple estates never file.

faqs.q: Do heirs pay tax when they sell an inherited house in Wisconsin?
faqs.a: They may owe income tax on the gain, meaning sale price minus basis. Wisconsin generally lets you deduct 30% of net capital gain on assets held over one year. The estate's tax preparer can work out basis and the likely result.

faqs.q: Is the Wisconsin transfer fee due when a house passes under a will?
faqs.a: No, Wis. Stat. 77.25(11) exempts transfers by will, descent or survivorship. The fee of 30 cents per $100 comes into play on a sale, and the price is what it is measured on.

faqs.q: Can a Wisconsin estate use an affidavit instead of probate for a house?
faqs.a: Only if the Wisconsin property subject to administration is worth no more than $50,000 gross. A named personal representative cannot take real estate by affidavit unless also an heir, the trustee of the decedent's revocable trust, or the guardian.
